title: First and second declensions

objectives.can: Parse and form nouns of the first and second declensions.
Recognise ten common first- and second-declension nouns.

explanation.summary: Latin nouns fall into five families called declensions, each with its own set of case endings. The first and second declensions are the largest, and most of the commonest nouns of the Bible belong to them. Learning to read the ending tells you the case and number of a word, and a headword's genitive tells you which family it belongs to.

sections.heading: What a declension is
body: A noun has a stem, which carries its meaning, and an ending, which carries its case and number. In *terram* the stem is terr- and the ending is -am (accusative singular). In *terrarum* the same stem takes -arum (genitive plural). To decline a noun is to give its forms in order.

Each noun also has a gender (masculine, feminine or neuter) which does not change: it belongs to the word. Gender is shown by the agreement of adjectives and pronouns, and often by the declension and the ending, but not always.

sections.heading: The first declension
body: The first declension has a stem in -a, and its nominative singular ends in -a. Almost all its nouns are feminine: *terra* (earth), *vita* (life), *gratia* (grace), *via* (way), *aqua* (water), *anima* (soul), *porta* (gate). A few, such as *propheta* (prophet), are masculine because they name men.
The dictionary lists a noun by its nominative and genitive singular. For the first declension the genitive ends in -ae, which is how you recognise it: terra, terr-ae.

sections.heading: The second declension
body: The second declension has a stem in -o. Its masculine nouns end in -us in the nominative singular: *filius* (son), *servus* (servant), *angelus* (angel), *annus* (year), *locus* (place). The Lord and God, *dominus* and *deus*, are of this family too. Its neuter nouns end in -um: *verbum* (word), *regnum* (kingdom), *templum* (temple). The genitive singular is -i for both.

The neuter has one rule that holds in every declension: the nominative, accusative and vocative of a neuter noun are the same, and in the plural they all end in -a. So a neuter form such as *verba* cannot tell you by its ending whether it is subject or object; the sentence does.
The vocative of masculine nouns in -us is -e: *domine*, "O Lord". Nouns in -ius shorten this to -i (*fili*, "O son"). Everywhere else the vocative is the same as the nominative.

sections.heading: Forms that look alike
body: Many endings serve for more than one case. In the first declension -ae is genitive singular, dative singular and nominative plural, and -a is nominative and ablative singular. In the second, -o is dative and ablative singular. In both declensions -is is dative and ablative plural. You choose among the possibilities by looking at the rest of the sentence: a preposition such as *in* or *cum* points to the ablative, a verb of giving to the dative, and a noun that follows another noun to the genitive.

The analysed texts in the library are tagged by machine. Where a form could be several cases at once, the analysis leaves the case undecided, and those words are not used in the questions. That is why the tables below may show a dash for a form that does occur. For example the genitive singular of *terra* is terr-ae, the dative is terr-ae, and the nominative plural is terr-ae; the nominative plural of *filius* is fili-i, its genitive singular is fili-i, and its accusative singular is fili-um. You will meet all of these in the texts.

sections.heading: Two irregular nouns
body: *Deus* (God) has no vocative singular of its own: the nominative form is used when God is addressed. In the plural it is irregular, with forms such as dii and diis. These forms are not shown in the tables below because the analysis leaves them undecided. *Dominus* is regular. *Filia* (daughter) and *anima* (soul) take -abus, not -is, in the dative and ablative plural (*filiabus*, *animabus*), an old habit that kept them distinct from the masculine *filius*; it is not always followed in later texts.

misunderstandings: An ending is not a case. The ending -a is nominative or ablative singular in terra, but nominative or accusative plural in verba. Always ask what declension the noun is before you decide.
Gender follows the word, not the ending. *Agricola* (farmer) and *propheta* (prophet) look feminine but are masculine. Do not guess from -a.

The -us ending is not always second declension. Some nouns in -us belong to the third and fourth declensions (*tempus*, *spiritus*), and their endings differ. Check the genitive: -i points to the second declension.
The plural of a neuter noun in -a is not a first-declension feminine singular. *Verba* is the plural of *verbum*, 'words'.

deeper.heading: Why the endings are so alike
body: In the earliest Latin the first declension had a form in -ai for the genitive singular and -ais for the dative plural. These simplified in time to -ae and -is. Spelling in the medieval and Vulgate editions often writes -ae as -æ, as in *gratiæ*; the library's analysis treats the two as the same ending. Our editions print no macrons, so the length of the vowels is not marked.

examples.analysis: *terram* is the accusative singular of *terra*, a first-declension feminine: terr-am. It is the object of *creavit*, 'created'. The ending -am is the plainest sign of the first declension accusative.

examples.analysis: *gloriam* appears twice, both times accusative singular: glori-am. The first is the object of *vidimus*, 'we saw'; the second repeats it in apposition. The genitive of the same word in this verse's last words is *gratiæ* (from *gratia*), which is the same shape as the dative: the ending -æ is spelled -ae in other editions.

examples.analysis: *nidos* is accusative plural of *nidus*, a second-declension masculine: nid-os, the object of *habent*. *Filius* is nominative singular, the subject of the second clause: fili-us. Note how the two masculine forms differ: -os marks the accusative plural, -us the nominative singular.
